title: Assessing heat loss from an end-terrace flank wall
subtitle: Measuring the extra exposure and deciding whether solid wall insulation is worthwhile
excerpt: The exposed flank wall of an end-terrace house loses roughly 25 to 40% more heat than the same wall in a mid-terrace. This guide shows how to estimate that extra loss, how to identify if the wall is cavity or solid, and how to compare the options for reducing it.
sourceNotes: BRE Report BR 443 (Conventions for U-value calculations, 2019) for standard wall U-values by age band and construction. Energy Saving Trust guidance on end-of-terrace heat loss. gov.uk Building Regulations Approved Document L1B for retrofit U-value targets.

glossaryTerms.definition: A measure of how quickly heat passes through a building element. Lower is better. Units are W/m²K.
Insulation added to a wall that has no cavity: either external (applied to the outside face) or internal (attached to the inside face).
A path through a building element that conducts heat more readily than the surrounding material, creating a cold spot.

content.text: An end-terrace house has one extra external wall that a mid-terrace does not. The exposed flank wall is typically 6 to 9 m wide and 4 to 6 m tall: 24 to 54 m² of wall with no neighbour on the other side. That wall can lose 40 to 140 W for every degree of indoor-outdoor temperature difference, depending on how it was built.
Whether insulating that wall pays back depends on the construction type, the current
U-value
, and the heating pattern. This guide walks through the assessment. It does not replace a professional survey, but it identifies whether a survey is worth commissioning.
Step 1: identify the wall construction

The simplest test is the brick pattern. Cavity walls built after around 1920 typically show a stretcher bond: all bricks are laid lengthways. Solid walls, common before 1920, often show a mixed bond with headers (bricks laid end-on). Cavity width can also be confirmed by drilling a small exploratory hole and inserting a bent coat-hanger.
A pre-1920 solid brick wall has a U-value of around 2.1 W/m²K if 220 mm thick, or 1.7 W/m²K if 340 mm thick.
A 1920s to 1980s cavity wall without insulation has a U-value of around 1.5 to 1.6 W/m²K.
A post-1990 cavity wall with partial-fill insulation has a U-value of around 0.45 to 0.6 W/m²K.
Step 2: measure the wall area

Measure the gross external area of the flank wall: width from corner to corner, height from ground level to the eaves. Subtract window and door openings. A typical 1930s end-terrace flank wall is around 6 m wide and 5 m tall (30 m² gross) with a 1.2 m² side door and two 1.5 m² windows, leaving around 27 m² of wall area.
Step 3: calculate the annual heat loss

Annual heat loss formula: kWh = U-value × area (m²) × degree-days × 24 / 1,000. Central England averages around 2,000 degree-days a year. A 27 m² solid brick wall at 2.1 W/m²K loses: 2.1 × 27 × 2,000 × 24 / 1,000 = 2,722 kWh a year through the flank wall alone.
Step 4: calculate the saving from insulation
The Part L1B target for
solid wall insulation
retrofit is 0.30 W/m²K. A typical 90 mm external system achieves 0.28 W/m²K. Using the same formula: 0.28 × 27 × 2,000 × 24 / 1,000 = 362 kWh a year. The saving is 2,722 − 362 = 2,360 kWh a year.
Common variations
North or east-facing flank wall: rain exposure is higher on these faces. External insulation must use a render or cladding rated for the exposure zone (BS 8414).
Flank wall next to an alleyway: no neighbour on the other side, but the passage limits access for external insulation work.
Unfilled cavity on the flank wall: cavity-fill is often the most cost-effective upgrade. It costs roughly a third of external insulation for a similar U-value gain.
When to call a professional
External wall insulation needs a surveyor. Fixings, render, window detailing, and
thermal bridge
treatment all need professional specification. Internal wall insulation is more DIY-friendly but still needs a dew-point check and a vapour control layer.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: The wall feels damp inside on the ground floor corner
rows.cause: Thermal bridge at the floor-wall junction, or rising damp combining with interstitial condensation
rows.fix: Have the junction surveyed before adding internal insulation. Adding insulation on the inner face raises condensation risk at the perimeter if the floor-wall junction is not treated at the same time.

rows.symptom: Calculation gives a very short payback but installer quotes suggest much longer
rows.cause: The simplified degree-days calculation assumes the wall is always heated; actual payback depends on how many hours per day the heating runs
rows.fix: Divide the annual heat loss figure by the daily heating fraction (e.g. if the house is heated 8 h/day, multiply by 8/24 = 0.33) before comparing against installation cost.
